---
title: "Scientist perception ratings"
author: "Sarah Segall"
date: today
format: html
---

DataPipe saves **one CSV file per participant**. This document reads all of
them, removes participants who failed the attention check or look like an AI
filled in the survey, and then runs the confirmatory test from Markowitz
(2024), Study 2: are scientists who wrote AI summaries rated as more
trustworthy than scientists who wrote PNAS summaries?

## Load packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)  # reading, wrangling, and plotting data
library(here)       # file paths relative to the project folder
library(lme4)       # lmer() for mixed models
library(lmerTest)   # adds p-values to lmer() results
library(assertthat) # assert_that() stops the document if something is wrong
```

```{r}
install.packages("renv", repos = "https://rstudio.r-universe.dev")
```

## Read in all the data files

The main study files are in `data/raw/main/` inside this project. When more participants
finish, copy their files into that folder and they will all be read in.

DataPipe also saves `.partial.json` files. These are backups from people who had not finished yet or never finished. So I only read the `.csv` files.

```{r}
files <- list.files(here("data", "raw", "main"),
                    pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) #to save only the csvs, not the partial jsons
files
```

`read_csv()` can read a whole list of files and stack them into one table.

```{r}
all_data <- read_csv(files, show_col_types = FALSE)
```

Each participant who finished should have the same number of rows.

```{r}
all_data %>%
  count(subject_id)
```

## Check 1: the attention check

Participants were asked to select "Strongly disagree" (a 1 on the 1-7 scale) that was mixed in with the AI attitudes and experiences survey . Anyone who chose anything but "Strongly disagree" failed this attention check.

```{r}
attention <- all_data %>%
  filter(measure == "attention_check") %>%
  select(subject_id, response)

attention
```


```{r}
# keep the IDs of the people who passed the attention check
passed_ids <- attention %>%
  filter(response == "1") %>%
  pull(subject_id)

passed_ids

length(passed_ids)
```

## Check 2: signs of AI agents taking the study

The three open-ended questions in the AI survey recorded how each answer was typed:

- `honeypot_triggered`: the first open-ended question had a hidden sentence, which was
  invisible to participants, and this sentence was telling an AI to use the word "periwinkle". `TRUE` means
  the answer contained that word.
- `paste_count`: how many times text was pasted into the box.
- `keystrokes` vs. `response_length`: someone who types their answer presses
  about as many keys as there are characters. Far fewer keystrokes than
  characters means the text was inserted rather than typed.

```{r}
ai_checks <- all_data %>%
  filter(measure %in% c("ai_example_coursework", "ai_disasters", "ai_elaborate")) %>%
  select(subject_id, measure, honeypot_triggered, paste_count, keystrokes, response_length)

ai_checks
```

Flag an answer if the honeypot word appears, if anything was pasted, or if
fewer than half of its characters were typed.

```{r}
flagged_ids <- ai_checks %>%
  filter(honeypot_triggered == TRUE | paste_count > 0 | keystrokes < response_length / 2) %>%
  pull(subject_id)

flagged_ids
```

## Check 3: time to finish the study

The consent form says the study takes 5-30 minutes. We exclude anyone who
finished in under 5 minutes (too fast to have read and digested the summaries) or took over
60 minutes (double the longest expected time, so they likely left and came
back, and their ratings were not made in one sitting).

```{r}
# `time_elapsed` on the last screen (the debrief) is the total time in milliseconds
# dividing by 60,000 converts it to  minutes

times <- all_data %>%
  filter(measure == "debrief") %>%
  mutate(minutes = time_elapsed / 60000) %>%
  select(subject_id, minutes)

times
```

```{r}
# keep the IDs of the people who finished between 5 and 60 minutes

time_ok_ids <- times %>%
  filter(minutes >= 5, minutes <= 60) %>%
  pull(subject_id)

time_ok_ids

length(time_ok_ids)
```

## Keep only participants who passed all three checks

```{r}
clean_data <- all_data %>%
  filter(subject_id %in% passed_ids) %>% # `%in%` asks "is this ID in that list?"
  filter(!(subject_id %in% flagged_ids)) %>% # `!` means "not"
  filter(subject_id %in% time_ok_ids)

n_distinct(all_data$subject_id)    # participants before exclusions
n_distinct(clean_data$subject_id)  # participants after exclusions
```


## Sanity check: look at the cleaned data

```{r}
glimpse(clean_data)
```

```{r}
head(clean_data)
```

## Keep only the trustworthiness ratings

The `response` column also holds consent, demographic, and survey answers, so
R reads it as text. Once I keep only the trustworthiness ratings, I turn
`response` back into numbers with `as.numeric()`.

I also make `version` a factor with `"pnas"` first, so the model compares GPT *to* PNAS (the same direction as the original paper).

```{r}
trust <- clean_data %>%
  filter(measure == "trustworthy") %>%
  mutate(response = as.numeric(response)) %>%
  mutate(version = factor(version, levels = c("pnas", "gpt"))) %>%
  select(subject_id, stimulus_id, version, response)

trust
```

## Sanity checks with `assert_that()`

Each `assert_that()` states something that SHOULD be true if the data were
recorded and cleaned correctly. If any one is false, rendering stops with an
error, so I find out right away instead of getting a wrong answer later.

```{r}
# 1. One file per participant, and no participant appears twice
assert_that(n_distinct(all_data$subject_id) == length(files))

# 2. Everyone who finished went through the same 99 screens/questions
assert_that(all(count(all_data, subject_id)$n == 99))

# 3. Exclusions can only remove people, never add them
assert_that(n_distinct(clean_data$subject_id) <= n_distinct(all_data$subject_id))

# 4. Nobody who failed a check is still in the clean data
assert_that(all(clean_data$subject_id %in% passed_ids))
assert_that(!any(clean_data$subject_id %in% flagged_ids))
assert_that(all(clean_data$subject_id %in% time_ok_ids))

# 5. Each participant rated exactly 5 summaries...
assert_that(nrow(trust) == 5 * n_distinct(trust$subject_id))

# 6. ...on 5 different topics (nobody saw both versions of the same topic)
topics_per_person <- trust %>%
  distinct(subject_id, stimulus_id) %>%
  count(subject_id)
assert_that(all(topics_per_person$n == 5))

# 7. There are 5 topics in total
assert_that(n_distinct(trust$stimulus_id) == 5)

# 8. Every rating is a whole number from 1 to 7, with nothing missing
assert_that(!any(is.na(trust$response)))
assert_that(all(trust$response %in% 1:7))

# 9. Version is only "pnas" or "gpt", in that order
assert_that(!any(is.na(trust$version)))
assert_that(identical(levels(trust$version), c("pnas", "gpt")))
```

## One row per participant

```{r}
# pivot wider
trust_wide <- trust %>%
  group_by(subject_id, version) %>%
  summarise(mean_rating = mean(response), .groups = "drop") %>%  # one average per person per version
  pivot_wider(names_from = version,       # the version names become column names
              values_from = mean_rating)  # and the averages fill them in

trust_wide
```

## Sanity check graphs

### How long did people take?

This uses every participant (before exclusions), so I can see who the 5- and
60-minute cutoffs remove. The dashed lines are the cutoffs.

```{r}
times %>% ggplot(aes(x = minutes)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "black", fill = "grey80", binwidth = 15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(5, 60), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue", linewidth = .8) +
  labs(title = "How long participants took to finish the study",
       x = "Minutes to finish",
       y = "Number of participants") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

```{r}
mean(times$minutes)
```

```{r}
sd(times$minutes)
```

### How were the trustworthiness ratings spread out?

Ratings can only be whole numbers from 1 to 7, so each bar is one point on the scale.

```{r}
trust %>% ggplot(aes(x = response)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "black", fill = "grey80", binwidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of all trustworthiness ratings",
       x = "Trustworthiness rating (1 = not at all, 7 = very)",
       y = "Number of ratings") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

### Did each topic get rated in both versions?

Versions were assigned at random, so the counts per topic will not be exactly
even, but every topic should have some GPT and some PNAS ratings.

```{r}
trust %>% ggplot(aes(x = stimulus_id, fill = version)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge", color = "black") +
  # blue = PNAS, orange = GPT (Okabe-Ito colors, readable with color blindness)
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(pnas = "#0072B2", gpt = "#E69F00"),
                    labels = c(pnas = "PNAS\n(human-written)", gpt = "GPT\n(AI-written)")) +
  labs(title = "Number of ratings for each topic and version",
       x = "Topic (stimulus ID)",
       y = "Number of ratings",
       fill = "Summary version") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

### Version 1

```{r}
# each participant's average rating for each version (one row per person per version)
person_means <- trust %>%
  group_by(subject_id, version) %>%
  summarise(mean_rating = mean(response), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r}
person_means %>% ggplot(aes(x = version, y = mean_rating)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = version), alpha = .4, outlier.shape = NA, width = .4) +
  geom_line(aes(group = subject_id), color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(color = version), alpha = .4, size = 3) +
  # blue = PNAS, orange = GPT (Okabe-Ito colors, readable with color blindness)
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(pnas = "#0072B2", gpt = "#E69F00")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(pnas = "#0072B2", gpt = "#E69F00")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(pnas = "PNAS\n(human-written)", gpt = "GPT\n(AI-written)")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1, 7), breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(title = "Trustworthiness ratings",
       x = "Summary version",
       y = "Average trustworthiness rating (1-7)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

trust %>% ggplot(aes(x = version, y = response)) +

## Exploratory: one row per participant

These use `trust_wide`. They are only descriptive. The confirmatory test is the
mixed model below, which uses the long `trust` data.

```{r}
# each person's GPT-minus-PNAS difference (positive = trusted GPT more)
trust_wide <- trust_wide %>%
  mutate(diff = gpt - pnas)

trust_wide

# descriptive stats (min, median, mean, sd, n...)
# `mosaic::` uses favstats() without loading all of mosaic,
# which would replace dplyr's count()
mosaic::favstats(trust_wide$gpt)
mosaic::favstats(trust_wide$pnas)
mosaic::favstats(trust_wide$diff)
```

```{r}
trust_wide %>% ggplot(aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "black", fill = "grey80", binwidth = .5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Each participant's GPT minus PNAS trustworthiness",
       x = "GPT average minus PNAS average (right of 0 = trusted GPT more)",
       y = "Number of participants") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

```{r}
# do people who trust PNAS scientists more also trust GPT scientists more?
trust_wide %>% ggplot(aes(x = pnas, y = gpt)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5, size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(title = "Participants' average PNAS vs. GPT trustworthiness",
       x = "Average PNAS rating (1-7)",
       y = "Average GPT rating (1-7)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

```{r}
# simple paired comparison (exploratory only)
t.test(trust_wide$gpt, trust_wide$pnas, paired = TRUE)
```


## Confirmatory test

```{r}
# Each participant rated several summaries, and each summary was rated by
# several participants, so the ratings are not independent. Like the original
# paper, I use a linear mixed model with a random intercept for participant
# (`1 | subject_id`) and for stimulus (`1 | stimulus_id`).

trust_model <- lmer(response ~ version + (1 | subject_id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
                    data = trust)

summary(trust_model)

# estimate is B --> unstandardized coefficient.
# interpretation: how much higher or lower on the 1-7 scale GPT summaries were rated than PNAS summaries
# original study B for GPT = 4.70, while PNAS was 4.42, *t* = 4.62, *p* < .001
```

## Robustness check: the same test with every participant

```{r}
# The original study did not exclude anyone, so I also run the exact same
# test on `all_data` (before any exclusions). If both tests point the same
# way, my exclusions did not change the conclusion.

trust_all <- all_data %>%
  filter(measure == "trustworthy") %>%
  mutate(response = as.numeric(response)) %>%
  mutate(version = factor(version, levels = c("pnas", "gpt"))) %>%
  select(subject_id, stimulus_id, version, response)

trust_all %>%
  group_by(version) %>%
  summarise(mean_rating = mean(response),
            sd_rating = sd(response),
            n_ratings = n())
```

```{r}
trust_all_model <- lmer(response ~ version + (1 | subject_id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
                        data = trust_all)

summary(trust_all_model)
```
